studies.title: Moths And Carded Wool
studies.meaning: A name is given with no explanation, repeated as a bare question, then repeated a third time inside the formula asking what could tell you what it is. Three lines for one word, so the chapter delays before showing anything at all. Then two comparisons arrive, and both reduce rather than enlarge. People become like scattered moths; mountains become like wool teased apart for spinning. The commentators note the pairing: the lightest living thing and the heaviest dead one are made equally weightless in consecutive lines.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The chapter belongs with the short descriptions of the last day that work through image rather than argument, addressed to an audience that treated the whole idea as a figure of speech. The classical sources report no occasion for it. They note instead that the surah supplies its own vocabulary, since two of its central words appear almost nowhere else in the Book.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a root of knocking violently, the same root that gives the word for a calamity striking a people. The day is named by an impact and a sound rather than by a date.

A collective for the insects that swarm a lamp at night, flying without direction and colliding with each other. It occurs only here in the Quran, and what it supplies is disorder rather than smallness.
Wool that has been teased apart for spinning, and coloured. The word appears twice in the Quran and both times describes mountains on that day, so the image is a fixed one rather than improvised.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both comparisons come from inside the house. A lamp in a tent drew moths all evening, and anyone sitting up late had watched them collide and scatter with no pattern to it. Wool was carded by hand before spinning, pulled apart until a heavy fleece became something that lifted on a breath. Two ordinary domestic sights, and one of them is applied to mountains.
studies.didYouKnow: The name given to the day is repeated three times in the first three lines: once as a bare noun, once as a question, once inside the formula asking what could inform you of it. The word occurs only once anywhere else in the Quran, so three of its four appearances in the entire Book are in these opening lines.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the two comparisons establish is not destruction but the collapse of scale. Heavy and light stop being different, and that difference is what every human calculation is built on: which things matter, which can be moved, which will still be there tomorrow. Cancelling it is the necessary preparation for what comes next in the chapter, where weight is measured again and assigned on a different basis entirely.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same wool image for the mountains, with the sky like molten metal beside it.
Contains the only other use of this name for the day, saying two earlier peoples denied it.
Answers a question about the mountains by saying they will be scattered and the ground left level.

studies.applyIt: Pick up the heaviest thing in the room you are sitting in and hold it for ten seconds. Feel how much of your sense of what is real comes from weight: what can be moved, what cannot, what will still be here next year. The surah spends two lines removing exactly that, and it starts with a moth.

studies.title: Heavy Scales, Light Scales
studies.meaning: Two conditions in matching grammar, separated by one pair of verbs: heavy and light. What is being weighed is never named. The text says only that his scales are heavy, and the word is a plural, which the commentators read either as several weighings or as the balance and its weights together. The first outcome is a life described as content. The second is stranger: his mother is a pit. Classical readers explain it as an Arabic idiom in which a man's refuge is called his mother, so his shelter is an abyss.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Balances were the instrument of the marketplace this audience lived in, used for grain, for silver measured by weight rather than counted, and for anything sold by the measure. The idea of weighing a life was already present in the religious vocabulary circulating in the region, and the classical sources report no particular occasion for these lines.

keyTerms.note: A plural covering both the balance itself and the weights placed in it, so the Arabic leaves open whether several weighings happen or one instrument has many parts. Commentators record both readings.

keyTerms.gloss: a life, a way of living
keyTerms.note: Not the ordinary word for life but one naming the manner in which a life is lived. Paired with a participle of contentment, it describes an existence that is satisfied rather than one that merely continues.
An active participle from the verb to fall, occurring only here in the Quran. It is read both as a name for the fire and as a plain description of something a person drops into.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Mecca was weighed. Silver was not counted out but measured on a balance, grain was sold by the measure, and a trader carried his own weights. The balance was therefore the object most often argued about and most commonly suspected of being rigged, and a merchant's whole reputation rested on his. An audience hearing about scales heard a familiar instrument that everyone distrusted in somebody else's hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the losing outcome occurs only once in the whole Quran, and the surah immediately treats it as needing explanation, asking in the next line what it is before answering in two words. So the chapter uses its explanatory formula twice in eleven very short lines, once for the day at the beginning and once for the destination at the end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures rather than itemises. No sin is named and no virtue is named; there is only a net weight, which makes the verdict fall on a life taken whole rather than on any single thing in it. The losing outcome is also described as somewhere a person falls into rather than somewhere he is sent, so the motion in that sentence stays on his side of it.

crossReferences.why: States the same measure directly, that the weighing on that day is the truth and heaviness is success.
Gives the identical pair of outcomes, heavy scales and light, in matching sentences.
Describes the scales themselves as set in place, with nothing omitted however small its weight.

studies.applyIt: Instead of listing what you did well and badly today, try to feel the day as a single weight in your hand. It is an unfamiliar exercise and most people find it harder than the list. That difficulty is informative: the passage weighs a whole life and names not one item in it.

studies.title: Two Words For An Answer
studies.meaning: The question asked in the line before is answered here in two words: a fire, scorching. Classical commentators note the economy of it. Having built the whole chapter out of delay, naming the day three times before showing anything, the surah closes its second question immediately and then stops. The describing word is an active participle rather than an adjective, so what is named is a fire in the act of heating rather than a fire that happens to be hot. Nothing further is added.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the last line of a chapter of eleven ayat, several of which run to two or three words. The classical sources give no occasion for it and describe the surah's shape instead: a name repeated, a scene shown, a sorting made, a second question asked, and then the shortest answer the language allows before the chapter ends.

keyTerms.note: Given without the article, although the question just asked was definite. Commentators read the indefiniteness as magnifying rather than vague: a fire of a kind the hearer has no example of.
An active participle rather than a plain adjective, so the fire is described as heating rather than as hot. The same word closes a similar description in one other short chapter and nowhere else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire in an ordinary house was small, contained and useful: a cooking hearth, a lamp, a smith's coals kept alive under ash. The large fires anyone had seen were the ones that got away, in dry scrub or in a store of fodder, and everybody knew how fast those travelled. The word here belongs to the second kind, and it is left indefinite because no fire in their experience was meant to stand in for it.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula used in the line before, asking what could inform you of something, occurs a dozen times across the Quran. Only two chapters use it twice, and this is by far the shorter of them, fitting both uses into eleven lines: once for the name of the day at the start, once for the name of the destination at the end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The brevity is the argument. A chapter willing to spend three lines withholding the name of a day spends two words on the fire and then ends, which sets a proportion. Warning is given, and then the text declines to dwell on it. What is established is that these descriptions are not offered as spectacle, and a reader who wants more detail is being refused rather than served.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical two-word description for the same thing, in the other short chapter where it occurs.
Asks the same question about a different name for the fire and answers at slightly greater length.
Repeats the question twice over about the day of judgement before giving any answer at all.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much you want the surah to say more, and that it will not. Then notice that you do this with other subjects too: illness, debt, a difficult conversation, where more detail feels like more control. Try leaving one of them at two words today and see whether anything is actually lost.
